[PAPER_0065, relevance_score=0.367] Hypotheses and Significance of the Present Work

In Studies 3 and 4, we shifted our focus to shared discrimination with the outgroup as a mechanism facilitating cue efficacy. To this end, in Study 3, we directly manipulated perceptions of shared discrimination with LGBT persons, and our preregistered hypothesis was that the cue aimed at LGBT persons would promote organizational safety and Black procedural fairness when shared discrimination was salient.

[PAPER_0066, relevance_score=0.241] Given that stigma solidarity scholarship has found that shared discrimination fosters intraminority connections (Cortland et al., 2017), in Study 3, we also included intraminority solidarity as an exploratory measure (i.e., no preregistered hypothesis).

Taken together, the present set of studies demonstrated the utility of organizational diversity cues among Black women and advanced our understanding of how to best facilitate Black women's organizational safety and procedural fairness.

[PAPER_0071, relevance_score=0.481] Similarities in Methodology Across Studies

We utilized a similar methodology across all experiments, which we describe here. All studies were approved by the institutional review board at the India R. Johnson's institution, and all participants were recruited from Prolific. Participants began the experimental session by providing informed consent and ended the session by completing manipulation checks and demographics before being thanked and debriefed. Apart from Studies 4-5b, all studies were advertised as "an impression of companies," and we utilized a fictitious consulting company across experiments.

[PAPER_0077, relevance_score=0.390] In the present experiment (and all subsequent ones), we utilized custom screeners to advertise our study to cisgender and heterosexual Black women and those not participating in other studies in the present work.

[PAPER_0084, relevance_score=0.361] Data Exclusions

We excluded a total of 32 participants for failing attention checks or indicating they did not identify as Black, heterosexual, and cisgender women. We also utilized a manipulation check at the end of the study to remove an additional 30 participants who failed to correctly answer two questions about the featured news article, leaving us with a final sample of 364.

[PAPER_0085, relevance_score=0.359] Participants and Sensitivity Analysis

Black women participants were paid $2.38 (approximately $9.50/hr) for a 15-min study. A post hoc power sensitivity analysis indicated that with a between-subjects ANOVA with four groups, at 95% power, with a sample size of 364, we were adequately powered to find a small (f = 0.19) effect size at p < .05.

[PAPER_0081, relevance_score=0.436] Method

Power Analysis

Sample size was informed by a pilot study examining our shared history manipulation.8 Our pilot test revealed an effect size of d = 0.56 among Black women participants for the difference between the shared history with the LGBT movement versus shared history with the labor movement conditions. We utilized this effect size for a two-factor, between-subjects experimental design with 95% power.

[PAPER_0082, relevance_score=0.455] Our power analysis revealed we would need approximately 54 participants per condition (i.e., 216 participants) using the following parameters: test family = F test, ANOVA (main effects and interactions); f = .25 (medium-sized effect); α = .05, 1 - β = 0.95; numerator df = 1; number of groups = 4. To account for failed manipulation checks and exclusions and to ensure we were adequately powered to detect the predicted interaction (Anderson et al., 2017), we aimed to retain a minimum sample of 326.

[PAPER_0083, relevance_score=0.317] Thus, we recruited 426 participants.

[PAPER_0084, relevance_score=0.345] Data Exclusions

We excluded a total of 32 participants for failing attention checks or indicating they did not identify as Black, heterosexual, and cisgender women. We also utilized a manipulation check at the end of the study to remove an additional 30 participants who failed to correctly answer two questions about the featured news article, leaving us with a final sample of 364.
